hints: Focus on what dilute ammonia does to each silver halide, since only one of them dissolves in dilute ammonia.
Notice Q is described as yellow and stays undissolved, while R is reprecipitated as white from the filtrate, so work out which halides these colours match.
Remember how concentrated sulfuric acid reacts differently with chloride, bromide and iodide, from steamy HCl to oxidised bromine and iodine vapours.
walkthrough:
**Use dilute ammonia to separate the mixture**

Think of dilute $\text{NH}_3$ as a test for solubility. $\text{AgCl}$ dissolves to form the complex ion, but $\text{AgBr}$ and $\text{AgI}$ do not.

$$\text{AgCl(s)} + 2\text{NH}_3\text{(aq)} \rightarrow [\text{Ag(NH}_3)_2]^+\text{(aq)} + \text{Cl}^-\text{(aq)}$$

**Identify Q and R from colours**

The filtrate contains the dissolved $\text{AgCl}$. Adding $\text{HNO}_3$ destroys the complex and reprecipitates white $\text{AgCl}$, so R is $\text{AgCl}$.

The undissolved solid Q is yellow. $\text{AgI}$ is yellow while $\text{AgBr}$ is cream, so Q must be $\text{AgI}$. This tells us P was $\text{AgCl} + \text{AgI}$.

**Warm each halide with concentrated sulfuric acid**

Both first form the hydrogen halide:
$$2\text{AgX} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{Ag}_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{HX}$$
Then oxidising power matters. $\text{HCl}$ is not oxidised, so you see steamy white fumes of $\text{HCl}$. $\text{HI}$ is a strong reducing agent and is oxidised to violet $\text{I}_2$ vapour.

So Q ($\text{AgI}$) gives violet fumes and R ($\text{AgCl}$) gives steamy fumes.

options.A: Violet for Q is right for AgI, but orange fumes mean Br2 from AgBr. There is no AgBr here because Q is yellow not cream and R is white AgCl, so orange fumes cannot appear.
options.B: Q is AgI which gives HI then violet I2 fumes with concentrated H2SO4. R is AgCl which gives steamy white HCl fumes that are not further oxidised. This matches perfectly.
options.C: This swaps the two results. Steamy fumes belong to the chloride R, not to the iodide Q, and violet fumes belong to the iodide Q, not to the chloride R.
options.D: Steamy fumes for R is correct for AgCl, but orange fumes for Q would mean AgBr. Q is described as yellow and insoluble in dilute ammonia, which points to AgI giving violet fumes, not AgBr.
